name: Rocky shore
notes: Sea cliffs and rocky coasts: spray-zone lichens and salt-tolerant cushion/rosette herbs in crevices, wind-shaped scrub above, and brown seaweeds (rockweed, kelp) in the intertidal. Drawn on North Atlantic (Britain, Norway, New England), Pacific NW and Mediterranean cliffs; seaweeds flagged underwater.

canopy.name: Monterey cypress

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal: 3-5 needle-like cotyledons, then whorls of soft, spreading, blue-green needle-like juvenile leaves for the first year or so before the tight, rope-like scale leaves take over. Young trees are dense, narrow bright-green cones or columns with branches to the ground; the flat-topped, wind-sculpted crowns of the headlands come only after decades.
growth.source: USDA Woody Plant Seed Manual (Cupressus: C. macrocarpa pollinated in March, cones ripen 15-18 months later, cone crops usually begin before age 10, ~140 seeds/cone, 35-day germination tests, epigeal). Growth rate (fast when young) and longevity (the Lone Cypress is thought to be ~250 yr) estimated.

canopy.source: Monterey headlands; wind-flattened, fog-fed. Kew POWO.

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal seedling with 5-8 cotyledons, often perched on rotting nurse logs in coastal rainforest. Saplings are open, symmetrical cones with widely spaced branch whorls and stiff, very sharp, flattened blue-green needles standing out all around the twig; side branchlets droop.
growth.source: USDA Silvics (Harris): ~27 m within 50 years of reaching breast height on average SE Alaska sites; cones occasionally before 20 yrs, in stands from 20-40; good crops every 3-8 years; tolerant of shade (less than hemlock); may live 700-800 years

fruiting.source: USDA Silvics (pollen shed late April to early June; cones ripen the year they are pollinated, seed ripe late Aug-early Sep; dispersal from October, 73% within 6 weeks); cone size 5-10 cm from floras; crop and decay estimated

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal seedling with 3-6 cotyledons and a tuft of single primary needles, then short, twisted, paired needles. Young trees are dense, narrow cones with regular whorls. Open-grown shore pines become bushy, crooked and flat-topped; inland trees become slim, straight poles. Serotinous cones stay closed on the branches for decades.
growth.source: USDA Silvics (Lotan & Critchfield): viable seed commonly at 5-10 years; ~3.6 m at 20 years on medium sites; germination peaks in the 2 weeks after snowmelt; very intolerant of shade; shore pine small and short-lived; ages commonly 150-200+, old high-elevation trees to 400+

fruiting.source: USDA Silvics (reddish-purple female strobili in whorls of 2-5, mid-May to mid-July; cones mature Aug-Oct over a year after pollination, purple-green to light brown; Rocky Mountain cones serotinous, sealed until heated to 45-60 C and held for years; 10-24 seeds per cone)

growth.juvenile_note: Hypogeal: the acorn stays buried and roots deeply before a thin shoot appears. Seedlings and saplings carry holly-like leaves with spiny teeth, dark glossy green above and grey-felted below; adult leaves are smaller, entire and leathery. Young plants grow slowly in the shade of shrubs and trees, often bushy from browsing, before a single stem leads.
growth.source: European Atlas of Forest Tree Species (Quercus ilex: to 25 m, rarely 30; lifespan may exceed 1000 yr; shade-tolerant, regenerates under canopy); Wikipedia (young trees spiny-toothed, adults entire; Encina Tres Patas ~1,200 yr); growth rate and first-acorn age estimated

fruiting.source: European Atlas of Forest Tree Species (flowers May-Jun with new leaves; acorns ripen the first year, brown, 1.5-2 cm, a third to half in a light green cup; fall Nov-Jan; big crops every 4-6 yr); Wikipedia (1-3 acorns on a short stalk); sweet acorns of subsp. rotundifolia are eaten raw or roasted

growth.juvenile_note: Seedling: two oval cotyledons, then small soft trifoliate leaves like clover on a thin stem; soon the new shoots switch to rigid green spines and spine-tipped side shoots. By year two or three it is a dense, spiny, dark green cushion that then grows up and out into a thicket.
growth.source: USDA FEIS (Ulex europaeus): flowers in its 2nd or 3rd season, growth slow until year 2-3, max recorded age 29-46 yr, low shade tolerance, seedlings have trifoliate leaves; Wikipedia (lives about 30 yr, seed viable 30 yr)

fruiting.source: USDA FEIS (bee-pollinated; main flowering spring-early summer with a second flush in autumn; 1-8 seeds per pod); Wikipedia (coconut-scented yellow pea flowers 1-2 cm, hairy pods 2 cm dark purplish-brown that split explosively in hot weather). Ripening, hang and rot times estimated.

growth.juvenile_note: Tiny seedlings on rotting logs and stumps (light needed to germinate): two small cotyledons, then leathery, finely toothed oval leaves. Very slow at first (only 8-13 cm after 2-3 years); then spreads by layering and rhizomes into a thicket of zigzag, reddish, glandular-hairy stems with glossy, thick, egg-shaped evergreen leaves.
growth.source: USDA FEIS species review (Gaultheria shallon): germination in 27-45 days, light required; seedlings slow, 3-5 in after 2-3 yr; flowers only at >=5 yr; twigs live 16+ yr and rhizomes for centuries; shade-tolerant but less vigorous under dense canopy.

fruiting.source: USDA FEIS (flowers May-Jul, white to pink urn-shaped flowers on terminal bracteate racemes, ~6 per twig, bee and fly pollinated; hairy blue-black pseudoberries 6-10 mm ripen Aug-Oct and may persist to December, ~126 seeds each; regular good crops). Fruit set, rot and crop estimated.

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal seedling with two heart-shaped cotyledons, then long-stalked, soft, velvety, round and shallowly 5-7-lobed leaves. In year one it is a leafy rosette-like clump on a short thick stem; in year two (sometimes after another mild winter) it bolts into a woody-based, tree-like stem 1-3 m tall, covered in pink-purple, dark-veined flowers, and dies after seeding.
growth.source: Wikipedia Malva arborea (shrubby annual, biennial or perennial; 0.5-2 m, rarely 3 m; young plants may survive one or more mild winters, then die after flowering; flowers 3-4 cm in clusters of 2-7; hard-coated seeds viable for years, even after sea water); germination time estimated for hard-coated mallow seed

fruiting.source: Wikipedia (dark pink-purple flowers 3-4 cm, in axillary clusters of 2-7); fruit a flat disc-shaped schizocarp ('cheese') inside the persistent calyx that splits into 6-9 one-seeded wedges, as in other Malva; flowering June-Sept on British coasts; bee pollination, ripening and crop estimated from Malva

growth.juvenile_note: Starts as tiny greyish-green bumps and stubby straps on bare seaside rock above the splash zone. These lengthen into stiff, flattened, strap-like, forked branches that stand up in grey-green tufts 2-8 cm tall, dotted near the tips with round, pale, disc-shaped fruit bodies. It has no powdery soredia and spreads by spores and broken fragments.
growth.source: Wikipedia Ramalina siliquosa (grows well above the high-tide mark; chemotypes occupy different vertical zones; disc-like spore-producing bodies); growth (a few mm a year) and ages estimated from fruticose lichen growth studies

growth.juvenile_note: Spores germinate in a damp, salt-sprayed rock crack into a tiny heart-shaped green prothallus; months later the first fronds unroll: small, simple and rounded, then once-pinnate with a few blunt, toothed pinnae. The young plant is a small tuft of glossy, leathery, bright-green fronds on shiny dark stalks fanning out of the crevice.

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings are rare (germination is episodic, needing fresh water on saline ground); the seedling is a small tuft of short, stiff, grey-green leaves in two neat opposite ranks. Scaly rhizomes then run through the soil and send up rows of short, stiff, leafy shoots, forming a dense, low turf patch; male and female plants are separate.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Distichlis spicata (dioecious; seeds need stratification and scarification, germination rare and episodic, seedling survival 0-95% with falling salinity; rhizomes to 180 cm long, 10-25 cm deep; 15-45 cm tall, usually <30 cm; photosynthesis rises with light). Time to flowering and clone lifespan estimated.

ground.name: Red fescue

growth.juvenile_note: The seedling is a single hair-fine, dark green blade; it tillers into a small tuft in its first season and then creeps by slender rhizomes, so tufts run together into a close, springy sward. On salt-sprayed cliff tops it stays short and dense, with reddish leaf sheaths at the base.
growth.source: Stace 2019 New Flora of the British Isles and Rodwell 2000 (Festuca rubra: rhizomatous, culms 20-70 cm, the main grass of maritime cliff swards); seed germinates in 1-3 weeks; single shoots short-lived but clones very old (Harberd 1961 found a clone some 220 m across); shoot lifespan estimated

ground.source: Festuca rubra, red fescue: the grass of maritime cliff-top swards and salt-sprayed ledges around the North Atlantic (Festuca rubra-Armeria maritima maritime grassland, Rodwell MC8-MC12), and of grassland across the northern temperate zone; creeping, culms 20-70 cm, fine rolled leaves, reddish-purple panicles — Kew POWO; Rodwell 2000 British Plant Communities vol. 5; Stace 2019 New Flora of the British Isles.

ground.name: Seaside grimmia
ground.origin: North Atlantic and North Pacific coasts

growth.juvenile_note: Spores lodge in cracks of bare acid rock above the barnacles and sprout a green film, then tiny upright shoots. These pack into small, hard, dark olive to blackish-green cushions 1-3 cm across, of stiff, narrow leaves without the silver hair-points of other Grimmias, topped in spring by short-stalked capsules.
growth.source: Atherton et al. 2010 Mosses and Liverworts of Britain and Ireland (Grimmia maritima: dense dark cushions on siliceous rocks in the spray zone, leaves without hair-points); growth rate and ages estimated

repro.note: spores by wind and water; no flowers; needs a wet film to reproduce, so spread reads moisture not pollinators
